projects.longDesc:
CineVerse is a movie and TV application built as a static single-page app. It tracks watch history down to individual episodes, monitors streaming availability across regions, and surfaces departures by differencing consecutive regional scans rather than relying on unsupported API departure dates.

The client is offline-first using Firebase Firestore, handling multi-device sync conflicts by maintaining separate watched and removed sets for every episode. Private lists use client-side PBKDF2-SHA256 derivation to lock content behind a PIN without storing secrets on the server.

Voice search runs natively via the browser's SpeechRecognition API, paired with a custom watchdog to handle silent failures. Routing is handled via static SPA configurations on Cloudflare Workers and Vercel to maintain clean URLs across client-side navigation.
projects.outcome: A dependable, offline-first application that maintains accurate watch states across devices, surfaces regional streaming shifts without relying on missing API data, and runs cleanly across multiple static hosts.
projects.problem: Tracking episode progress across multiple devices risked race conditions where concurrent writes overwrote each other's ticks. Additionally, asynchronous Firebase authentication meant direct URL loads rendered empty states before user libraries could resolve.
challenges: Preventing multi-device progress syncs from accidentally resurrecting un-ticked episodes or erasing concurrent updates.
Handling SPA fallback routing on Cloudflare Workers without triggering infinite redirect loops caused by wildcard rule conflicts.
Overcoming browser-specific silent failures in the Web Speech API during voice searches.
Reconstructing missing historical episode progress for shows watched before fine-grained tracking was introduced.
projects.desc: A movie and TV encyclopedia featuring offline-first Firebase sync, episode-level watch tracking, streaming departure warnings, and voice search.
highlights: Episode-level watch tracking with conflict resolution using separate watched and removed states per season.

projects.longDesc:
Password Manager, titled Secure Offline Vault, is a single-page password vault that runs entirely in the browser. A master password is stretched with PBKDF2 (SHA-256, 210,000 iterations) through the Web Crypto API, and the derived key encrypts the vault with AES-GCM before it is written to localStorage. Nothing is sent to a server.

Entries hold a title, username, password, URL, notes, tags and custom fields, with favourites, tag filters, search and a trash bin. Each entry keeps a short history of earlier passwords, and a generator builds new ones from crypto.getRandomValues with selectable character sets.

A security audit scores the vault and flags weak, common and reused passwords, as well as any older than 90 days. Copied secrets are cleared from the clipboard after 30 seconds, the vault locks itself after a period of inactivity, and a session log records recent actions. Encrypted backups can be exported and restored, and entries can be imported from CSV.

Arnav Island is a native Windows 11 app that sits at the top of the screen as an island, animated with physical spring motion. It shows real system information, plays and queues music with crossfades and word-timed lyrics, keeps a Shelf for files and a universal clipboard, and offers capture tools, file search, per-app volume and workspaces.

With the Arnav Island for Android companion, the phone and PC reach each other on the same Wi-Fi or across networks through a direct path or an end-to-end encrypted relay. Notifications arrive grouped by app and chat with replies from the keyboard, text messages can be answered from the PC, files move both ways, and screens can be shared in either direction.

It also tracks month-to-date spend for the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs using official organisation cost endpoints.

Every reading is kept in a local SQLite history, which feeds charts, a weekly report in plain English, a single usage score across providers and usage-pace forecasts such as "limit around 4:10 PM (likely 3:40–4:50 PM)". Forecasts disclose sample counts and variability and are suppressed when there isn't enough data. Token counts from Claude Code and Codex transcripts are shown against API prices, with model mix and weekly project budgets.

The app pairs with UsageNotch for Android over HTTPS pinned to the PC's own certificate, with optional encrypted internet sync through a secret gist in your own GitHub account. It ships as a single portable EXE that updates itself from GitHub Releases after verifying a signed update manifest.

You build routes between around 200 real cities and run trucks, trains, planes and ships along them.

projects.desc:
Voice, rediscovered.

A presence-first voice platform. Peer-to-peer, end-to-end encrypted by the browser itself, and architected so that the expensive parts of calling simply do not exist.
projects.longDesc:
Most calling software treats every conversation as a meeting: a link, a lobby, a calendar entry, a fifteen-minute minimum. Sonder puts voice back where it belongs — instant, ambient and low stakes.

Audio travels directly between devices. No media server sits in the middle, which means the operator of a Sonder deployment is structurally incapable of listening, and there is no per-minute meter to run. Firestore is used purely as a mailbox for the connection handshake — a few hundred bytes, then silence.

projects.longDesc:
PHOSPHENE is an interactive work of science fiction: the public observatory of the Phosphene Institute, which in 2236 picks up the Serein Signal, the memory of the Ithra, a civilisation that ended thirty-six thousand years ago, sent as seven narrow spectral lines. Every star, relic, world, glyph and sound on the site is generated in the browser.

The site is split into places: a scroll-driven descent to a ray-traced ring of light over a mirror-black sea, an explorable orrery with an epoch slider, twenty-four relics reconstructed as holograms, five stories with their own layouts, six working simulations, a live lunar array of 64 dishes with a real-time spectrogram, and a navigable constellation map that traces your own path.

Under the hood, a single persistent WebGL context renders behind every page. A custom engine on vanilla three.js swaps code-split scenes, adapts graphics quality to the GPU and measured frame times, and runs GPGPU particle systems of up to a million particles. Sound is synthesised with the Web Audio API, with each tone being a spectral line's light frequency transposed down forty octaves.

Every WebGL experience has an HTML equivalent, reduced motion is honoured, every page is prerendered for crawlers and visitors without JavaScript, and the site is installable as a PWA that works offline on anything already visited.

Sound is synthesised with the Web Audio API, and heavy work such as relic geometry and the receiver's FFT runs in Web Workers.

projects.longDesc:
Sentinel is a native Windows 11 app, built with WinUI 3 and .NET 10, that watches processor, graphics, memory, storage, battery, thermals, network, devices and reliability. It records history, learns baselines for your machine and flags anomalies, with a "What changed?" timeline, Time Machine and period comparison.

It is strictly read-only: it never overclocks, controls fans, writes to firmware, installs a kernel driver or changes system settings. Every value comes from a documented Windows interface or a vendor's read-only API and is labelled with its source. When a machine doesn't expose something, Sentinel says "Not exposed by this system" rather than estimating.

Ask Sentinel answers plain-language questions such as "Why did my PC restart today?" using a deterministic, evidence-based engine that labels each finding as Observed, Inferred, Possible or Unknown. An optional local Ollama model can rephrase answers, connecting only to loopback addresses with redacted evidence.

It works offline, needs no account, installer or administrator rights, and sends no telemetry. Updates come from GitHub Releases and are verified against an ECDSA P-256 signature before installing.

Monocular Light Injection is a standalone build of the TypeGPU example of the same name. It runs a small depth-estimation model entirely on the GPU, using WebGPU compute shaders written in TypeScript, against your camera or a photo, then relights the scene in real time around a light you can drag around.

The inference pipeline doesn't use ONNX: convolutions (im2col and Winograd) and selective-scan kernels are implemented directly as WebGPU compute work. A relighting renderer then shades the scene from the estimated depth and normals. On first load you pick a source, either your camera or a bundled demo photo, and a model size. Larger models are more accurate but slower to download and run.

This repository lifts the example out of Software Mansion's TypeGPU docs site into its own minimal Vite project. A new app shell replaces the docs site's React/Tailwind control panel. It checks for a real WebGPU adapter before loading anything heavy, and adds a control dock with live slider readouts, a segmented view switcher, a colour swatch, keyboard shortcuts, toasts and first-run hints. Model weights are fetched at runtime from a hosted, revision-pinned bundle.

projects.longDesc:
Watchalong Sync is a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers that keeps a full-length reaction video in one tab and the actual movie in another playing in lockstep. No more counting down "3, 2, 1, play", and no re-syncing every time the reactors pause to talk.

You link the two tabs, press Alt+Shift+S the moment the reactors hit play, then only touch the reaction's controls. Play, pause, scrub and speed changes are mirrored on the movie. When the reactors pause the film, Alt+Shift+P holds the movie still and resumes from the exact frame, and those pauses are saved and replayed on rewatches. Ads and buffering on either side make the other wait.

Under the hood, sync is a piecewise map from reaction time to movie time. A controller in the movie tab compares where the movie should be with where it is: it ignores drift under 40 ms, gently adjusts playback speed by up to 6 % for drift up to 1.5 s, and beyond that pauses, seeks ahead and starts at the exact moment the reaction catches up. Seek and start-up latencies are learned per site, and steady-state error is typically 5–15 ms.

Everything stays in the browser: no account, no servers, no analytics. Syncs can be shared with friends as a short code, and site-specific adapters handle quirks such as Netflix's player API, Prime Video's stream offset and Apple TV+'s shadow DOM.
projects.outcome: Released as v0.9.1 for Chrome and Edge, with unit and simulation tests for the drift controller and an end-to-end harness that drives the real extension in Chromium, asserting p95 error under 50 ms across play, pause, seek, speed changes, ads and buffering, plus a WCAG 2.1 AA audit of every surface.

You can orbit a detailed model built to published dimensions, inspect components with sourced facts, explode it into assemblies, look through the skin with X-ray and section planes, and walk both passenger decks across 469 seats.

The cockpit has eight live displays, an FCU and operable levers and overhead buttons. It is an educational approximation, not certified data or a training device, and is not affiliated with Airbus.

It runs on a Cloudflare Worker with D1. Stream failures are logged, a cron job re-checks catalogue files every 30 minutes, dead files are skipped automatically, and a /status page shows the dashboard.

Flick lets you control Android apps without touching the screen. A nod moves to the next reel, a smile likes it, and a double knock on the back of the phone goes back. It offers 37 gestures across head, face, hand, phone movement, volume buttons and experimental offline voice keywords, and each can be mapped to any action: swipes, taps, double-tap to like, back, home, screenshots, media controls and more.

Gestures are organised into per-app profiles with defaults for apps like Reels, YouTube, browsers and Kindle. Live calibration shows the signal and lets you set sensitivity, hold time, cooldown and a neutral pose. Extras include auto-scroll, a floating controller, recordable macros, a Quick Settings tile, mindful mode nudges, edge glow feedback and a camera badge that pauses Flick with one tap.

Everything runs on the phone. Camera frames are analysed in memory with Google's on-device MediaPipe models and never saved or uploaded, and the camera only runs inside apps with camera-gesture profiles. There are no accounts, ads, analytics or crash reporting; the only network request is an optional update check against GitHub Releases, verified by SHA-256 checksum and signing certificate before install.

Arnav Flight Radar is a web-based flight tracker that runs its own world simulation. About 15,000 aircraft from more than 230 real airlines fly roughly 100 real aircraft types between real airports. At around 340 airports they park on real stands at the right terminal and taxi along real, named OpenStreetMap taxiways, while live METAR and TAF weather chooses the runway in use and sets airport capacity.

The simulation covers a flight gate to gate: clearance and push-back, taxi with holding points and stop-bars, wake-turbulence departure spacing, published FAA procedures and airways in the US, oceanic tracks, closed airspace, holding, ILS or RNP approaches and turnaround. Bad weather, emergencies, crew duty limits, maintenance checks and wet leases add disruption, alongside general aviation, military traffic, helicopters and gliders.

Liquid Level is a spirit level that runs in the phone browser. Tilt the device and a body of liquid responds: it sloshes, overshoots and settles towards the true horizontal. The moment you're within 0.45° of level, the scene changes state. The water goes still, the light turns gold, a halo pulses out and the phone gives a short haptic tick.

The liquid is not a rotating image. A shallow-water solver runs 168 coupled columns at 60fps, so waves propagate and momentum carries the surface past level before it rests. Roll and pitch come from the gyroscope through `deviceorientation`. They are corrected for screen orientation and smoothed, then shown as a live degree readout and as a bullseye bubble that floats to the high side like a real vial.

The whole project is a single HTML file with no dependencies and no build step. On desktop, or when motion access is denied, it falls back to pointer preview: moving the cursor tilts the liquid.

SKYCOMMAND is a fully playable 2D airport air-traffic-control game for the browser. You land arriving aircraft, park them at gates, watch the turnaround, push them back, taxi to the runway and launch them, with one or two taps per action. You can also drag a line along the taxiways to draw a route, which snaps to valid paths.

The airport has two parallel runways, one-way taxiways, a 20-gate terminal with animated jet bridges, service vehicles, a day/night cycle and weather including rain, storms and fog. Modes range from Kids, which a 7-year-old can pick up straight away, to Pro ATC with runway conflicts, wake separation, fuel limits and emergencies, plus a Sandbox and a Daily Challenge.

Under the hood, a deterministic 20 Hz simulation is shared by the client and a Cloudflare Worker. Difficulty scales from Kids to Pro ATC. For the Daily Challenge, the client submits only its list of instructions, and a Durable Object per challenge date sanitises them, re-runs the simulation and stores the verified score in D1.

projects.problem: Real-world hide and seek on phones usually means broadcasting players' locations, which spoils the game and invites cheating through GPS spoofing.
projects.longDesc:
CloakRun is a native Android game that turns a neighbourhood, campus or park into a hide-and-seek arena. Hiders run and cloak, while seekers sweep with radar, follow clues and close in for a tag, all on a custom night map with luminous roads, radar sweeps and fog of war.

Privacy is the core design rule: a hider's exact GPS position stays on their device. The cloud and the seekers only see a fuzzed last-known zone that shrinks over time. Tagging relies on Bluetooth, so the seeker's phone has to actually hear the hider's rotating ephemeral ID at close range, which means spoofing GPS won't earn a catch.

The host draws the play area as a circle or polygon, or snaps to a park's real edge, with roads, rail, water and private land cut out as no-go zones. Friends join private lobbies with a six-character code, a QR code or an invite link. Powers such as Cloak, Decoy, Sonar Pulse and Freeze Trap are collected at cache points in the field and are never sold.

The latest release adds lobbies, onboarding with an age gate and stay-safe rules, anonymous accounts with optional Google linking, and Firestore and Realtime Database Security Rules tested against the emulator. Live matches are planned for the next release.

projects.longDesc:
Island draws a black, shape-shifting pill around the centred punch-hole camera on Android phones, tuned for the Samsung Galaxy S23+. One renderer handles every state (idle, compact, split, toast and expanded), morphing between them with closed-form spring physics that can be interrupted mid-flight without losing velocity.

It shows live activities from media players, notifications, calls, charging, Bluetooth devices, timers, navigation, deliveries and rides, calendar events, the flashlight and system toggles. Other apps can post their own activities through a local API. Gestures include tap, long-press, swipes, drag deformation and throw-to-dismiss, with themes from Classic Black to Glass and a custom rim, glow and highlight.

Version 1.2 adds a Blend with One UI screen: a seamless status bar that steps aside while a card is open, optional replacement of One UI pop-ups, and motion that follows the system animation scale. Island has no internet permission, no accounts, no analytics and no ads, and needs neither root nor an accessibility service.

It ships as two APKs with the same signature: a Lite edition that installs easily from a browser, and a full edition with notification access for music, calls, navigation and notifications.
projects.approach: A single Kotlin and Jetpack Compose renderer draws the island in every state, driven by analytic damped springs so transitions are frame-rate independent and can be interrupted while keeping their velocity. Shapes use continuous corners concentric with the display's rounded corners, with width-leads-height expansion and metaball split transitions. Activities come from MediaSession, the notification listener, system broadcasts and a local API. The app is split into full and lite product flavours with one signature, and GitHub Actions runs tests, builds both editions and verifies signing on each tagged release.

Driver Drowsiness & Distraction Detection is a college machine-learning project that runs entirely in the browser. It uses the webcam only after permission is granted and processes every frame on the device, with no API keys, accounts or cloud inference. Model files and the MediaPipe runtime are served from the project itself.

MediaPipe supplies 478 face and iris landmarks, blendshapes and a 3D pose matrix. From these the app derives eye closure, time-weighted PERCLOS, yawns, gaze and head pose, then an explainable temporal engine fuses severity, persistence and concurrence into a risk score. EfficientDet-Lite0 detects phone use, and the interface names the signal driving each score, including counterfactual explanations.

Alerts are spoken in English, Hindi, Kannada, Marathi, Tamil or Telugu, with vibration as a backup. A full-screen Drive Mode for a mounted phone keeps the screen awake, and the app installs as a PWA that works offline once models are cached.

On the research side, an int8 eye-state CNN and a drowsiness GRU trained on public datasets run in plain JavaScript. A Model Lab page compares them with the rule engine on live webcam frames and renders every experiment result. It is a research prototype, not certified safety equipment.

An apparent large gain from reusing an alert-state calibration turned out to be a camera-placement confound
Rejecting false alarms: yawns are judged by shape and duration so ordinary conversation is ignored, and the adaptive baseline is clamped so it cannot normalise a drowsy face
Desktop browsers do not always expose every language voice through the Web Speech API, so the app falls back to supplying the language code
Camera-only methods still fail with sunglasses, a hand over the mouth, or at night without infrared

projects.outcome: The eye-state CNN scored ROC-AUC 0.998 and F1 0.959 on DMD, and 92.6% accuracy out of domain on MRL Eye. On UTA-RLDD the best learned drowsiness model reached 53.3% three-class video accuracy against 47.8% for the rule engine (p = 0.018), below the published HM-LSTM's 65.2%. The app is live on GitHub Pages as an installable, offline-capable PWA, and remains a research prototype.
projects.approach: A hybrid architecture: MediaPipe finds 478 face and iris landmarks and a pose matrix, and EfficientDet-Lite0 detects phones. A deterministic temporal engine then calibrates to the driver over five seconds, tracks eye closure, PERCLOS, yawns, gaze and head pose over time, and fuses them into a risk score that names its main cause. Two learned models, an int8 eye-state CNN and a drowsiness GRU, were trained on public datasets with subject-aware splits and run in plain JavaScript. A learned model can only nudge the score, never override clear evidence. A feature-schema test keeps the app and the Python training pipeline in sync.

CineVerse for Android is the phone half of CineVerse, a film and television tracker rather than a streaming service. It uses the same Firebase project, documents and account as the website, so an episode ticked on the phone is ticked on the laptop too.

The app covers Home, Discover, My List, Stats and You, along with pages for titles, people, studios, franchises and box office figures. Episode tracking is the most designed interaction: tap the 48dp tick, swipe right to mark everything up to an episode, swipe left to un-tick, or long-press a season chip. It can also be done from a Glance home-screen widget, a notification's Mark watched button, or by asking Gemini on Android 16 through AppFunctions.

projects.problem: Metro riders in Indian and Gulf cities have little or no realtime data from operators, and many transit apps show estimated times without saying so, need an account or track the user.
projects.longDesc:
MetroPulse is a free, open-source Android app for metro networks in 26 cities across India, the Gulf, London and New York. It plans journeys offline, follows your train on a 3D map and rings a wake alert one or two stops before your destination, even with the screen off.

It never shows invented times. Every time is labelled Live, Scheduled or Approx., and where an operator publishes nothing, the app says so. London and New York get live arrivals and disruption alerts from TfL's Unified API and the MTA's GTFS-realtime feeds, fetched by the phone directly with no MetroPulse server in between. Delhi also shows live DTC and cluster buses near metro stations from Delhi Open Transit Data.

The app is built in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose and renders maps with MapLibre Native on OpenFreeMap tiles. City databases come from a Python pipeline that draws on OpenStreetMap and operator data, and city updates arrive weekly without an app update.

There is no account, analytics, ads or crash reporting, and location never leaves the phone. The app updates itself from GitHub Releases and checks each download's SHA-256 and signature.

projects.longDesc:
ImageVault is a cloud photo vault that finds duplicate photos. It catches exact copies, which are stored only once, as well as resized, compressed or edited versions and the same meme with different captions. You can compare matches with a slider, see the biggest space-wasters and delete the extras. Uploading a photo that is already stored gives a warning first.

Alongside duplicates, it groups burst shots and picks the sharpest, recognises the same person across photos, builds automatic albums such as Beach, Pets and Screenshots, and lets you search by describing a photo. Text on signs, receipts and boards is read in English, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and Kannada. Receipts and UPI payment screenshots become a small spending table that you can check, correct and export as CSV.

The AI models (CLIP, YuNet, SFace and PaddleOCR via ONNX Runtime and OpenCV) run inside the app, either in Azure App Service or on your own laptop as an edge worker, with no paid API and no photos sent to another company. On Windows the worker can run as a tray icon with Start and Stop.

The whole Azure setup (App Service, PostgreSQL, Blob Storage, Application Insights and a budget alert) is created with Terraform, and GitHub Actions tests every push and deploys main using OIDC and managed identities, so there are no storage keys or deployment passwords. A Cloud page shows live service health, month-to-date cost with a forecast, and storage used.

ATLAS ingests authoritative open feeds (USGS, GDACS, NOAA NHC, NASA EONET, Smithsonian GVP and NASA FIRMS), correlates reports into single stable incidents, tracks how they change, and renders everything on a real-time 3D Earth with Sentinel-2 cloudless imagery, the true sun position and city lights on the night side.

Every number is labelled Observed, Derived, Model estimate, Simulation or Unavailable, with its source and method named. Revisions and escalations go to an audit trail, and a Data Time Machine reconstructs what ATLAS knew at any past instant. Historical replays of eight major earthquake sequences ship offline for demonstrations.

The engine is Python with FastAPI and DuckDB (spatial and H3); the front end is React 19 and CesiumJS. It runs as a public web snapshot rebuilt every three hours, a local install with live streaming, or a Tauri desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux with the engine bundled. An optional local AI analyst runs through Ollama with read-only tools and cited answers.

Arnav Island for Android is a native Kotlin app that pairs with the Arnav Island app on Windows. It works directly over the same Wi-Fi and, once paired, from other networks too. It tries a direct path first (IPv6 or UDP hole punching) and falls back to end-to-end encrypted relaying through public MQTT brokers.

From the phone you can control what plays on your PC, with word-by-word lyrics, a volume dial and per-app volume. You can also use the phone as a trackpad and keyboard, view the PC's screen at up to 1440p, watch live processor, graphics, memory and battery figures, and send files and photos at full quality in either direction.

In the other direction, the island on your PC shows your phone's notifications and calls, battery and network details, and a universal clipboard. It can ring the phone with Find my phone. Version 1.13 adds browsing the phone's files from the PC, reading and replying to text messages, and unlocking the PC with your fingerprint.

There are no accounts, analytics or ads. Connections use ECDH P-256 key exchange and AES-256-GCM. The app updates itself from GitHub releases after checking each download's SHA-256 and signing certificate.

Arnav AI turns a prompt such as "45 minutes of energetic coding music" into structured constraints through Gemini (Firebase AI Logic), finds real songs cache-first and orders them along an energy curve, with an on-device fallback engine. You set taxes, the interest rate and trade policy, split the budget across healthcare, education, infrastructure, military, welfare and research, and pass laws such as universal healthcare or a carbon tax that take months and carry clear tradeoffs. Tap any number to see what is pushing it up or down, and move a slider to see a live 12-month forecast before committing, with Undo to take it back.

Beyond the economy there are trade deals, alliances, sanctions, a credit rating from AAA to C, home regions with separatists, nuclear weapons and the Doomsday Clock, dozens of events placed where they really happen, and elections that end with a legacy grade from A+ to F. Society systems are seeded from WHO, PISA, WRI, FAO, USGS, World Bank and SIPRI data.

The app is free, has no ads and works offline. It includes original synthesised sound and music, haptics, a guided first game, accessibility options and optional Firebase cloud saves, and it checks for and installs its own updates.

Built using a native WinUI 3 and .NET 10 shell paired with a React and TypeScript user interface rendered via WebView2, the application handles local data storage with SQLite and updates through Velopack. It includes a Performance Mode that suspends its interface to 0% CPU usage while a game is running.

The launcher features a command bar for filtering games locally, an Immersive Mode for full-screen play, and a Journal that tracks play history, heatmaps, and session performance metrics using tools like Intel PresentMon.

Image Converter Tool, titled ClipMorph Studio in the app, converts and edits batches of images entirely in the browser. Images can be pasted with Ctrl+V, read from the clipboard with a button, dragged in or picked from disk, and they collect in a queue with one marked as the active preview.

Edits include brightness, contrast, saturation, greyscale, sepia and blur, plus an optional text watermark with size, opacity and position. ApplyPilot is a native Windows app that searches for internships across the internet, tells you in plain words whether you can apply, and fills in application forms from your profile. It runs entirely on your own computer, needs no account, cloud service or API key, and follows one hard rule: it never guesses anything about you.

Autopilot reads the Simplify internship list, The Muse, Arbeitnow, Himalayas, Jobicy, Remotive, the Hacker News hiring thread and the careers boards of companies you follow on Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workday and others. It scores each job 0–100 against your verified profile, reads requirements such as degree, graduation window, experience, citizenship and visa sponsorship, and shows the sentence each came from. Anything it can't answer goes to an Inbox, where one answer unlocks every application that asks it.

When you're ready, one click opens the real application in your own Edge window, fills every field it has a verified answer for, attaches your approved CV, highlights what still needs you and stops. Automated submission is deliberately not implemented.

Around that core sit CV reading, tailored CVs with a colour-coded diff, optional local AI through Ollama for summaries and cover letters, a calendar with deadline alerts, offer comparison across currencies, IMAP email sync for tracking, and an installer that updates itself after verifying checksums.

projects.longDesc:
BlueChat Web is the browser version of the BlueChat messaging app. It is a single page built with Vue 3 and the Firebase JavaScript SDK, using Firebase Authentication for email and password accounts and Cloud Firestore for users, chats and messages.

After signing in, users see their conversations and a global public room. They can start a private chat with another registered user or create a named group, and the chat list updates in real time. Conversations can be pinned to the top of the list and searched, and messages are grouped by day.

Within a chat, users can reply to a specific message, add an emoji reaction, copy or delete messages and search the conversation. Private chats show whether the other person is online or when they were last seen, and read receipts can be turned off in settings. Users can also edit their name and status, block someone, clear a chat or delete their account.

ArnavOS, titled WebOS 2026 in the browser, is a desktop environment simulated inside a single web page. It opens on a lock screen with a clock and date, then shows a wallpaper, a top bar and a dock that launches eight apps: Notes, Calculator, Calendar, Files, Music, Terminal, Paint and Settings.

A custom window manager handles focus and stacking, dragging, resizing from any edge, minimising, maximising and snapping to the left or right half of the screen. Keyboard shortcuts close, minimise and maximise the active window, a command palette opens apps or locks the screen, and right-clicking the desktop brings up a context menu.

Files live in a small virtual file system saved to localStorage, alongside notes and preferences, so they survive a reload. The Music app plays a melody synthesised with the Web Audio API, the Terminal answers a handful of basic commands, Paint draws on a canvas, and light and dark themes are both available.

A web emulator of the Casio fx-991ES PLUS scientific calculator, with natural-textbook display, Casio precedence, S⇔D and calculus, built in React.
projects.longDesc:
A free web emulator of the Casio fx-991ES PLUS scientific calculator, focused on COMP mode. It reproduces the natural-textbook display with stacked fractions, radicals and superscript powers, along with the device's operator precedence, rounding, angle modes, memory and error behaviour.

Arithmetic runs at 15 digits internally and 10 on screen using decimal.js, with NORM1/NORM2, FIX and SCI formats. The S⇔D key toggles between decimals and exact fractions, surds such as √8 → 2√2, and π-multiples. Numerical integration uses adaptive Simpson and differentiation uses a Richardson-extrapolated central difference.

The calculator core is a pure, framework-agnostic TypeScript engine: a token model for nested input boxes, a Pratt/recursive-descent parser that applies Casio precedence, an evaluator and a formatter. A separate state machine handles the cursor, SHIFT/ALPHA, memory and SETUP, and the React UI sits on top. Engine, interactive flows and rendering are covered by an automated test suite.

It is an independent educational project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Casio.

challenges: Telling coefficient-style implicit multiplication apart from explicit multiplication, so 1÷2π gives 1/(2π) while 6÷2(1+2) gives 9
Finding exact surd forms from a numeric value rather than tracking them symbolically, which limits S⇔D to pure surds of the form (a√b)/c
Making box-based fraction and exponent entry practical: binary operators leave a denominator, exponent or radical box automatically, but stay inside numerators and parentheses
Numerical calculus, using adaptive Simpson for integrals and Richardson-extrapolated central differences for derivatives
projects.problem: The Casio fx-991ES PLUS behaves in specific ways that generic web calculators don't copy: its natural-textbook display, its precedence rules for implicit multiplication, its 15-digit internal and 10-digit displayed rounding, exact-form S⇔D results and its error handling. The aim was a browser version that behaves like the real device in COMP mode.
highlights: Natural-textbook display with stacked fractions, radicals, powers, |x| and 2D cursor editing
Casio precedence, including implicit multiplication: 1÷2π = 1/(2π) but 6÷2(1+2) = 9
S⇔D toggle to exact fractions, surds and π-multiples
∫dx integration, d/dx differentiation and CALC using stored variables
Memory with Ans/PreAns, M+/M−, and STO/RCL for A–F, X, Y, M
Physical keyboard support and a data-driven keypad layout checked against the real device
projects.approach: The calculator logic lives in a pure TypeScript engine with no framework dependency. A token model handles nested placeholders for fractions and roots. A Pratt/recursive-descent parser builds an AST using Casio precedence. An evaluator computes results with decimal.js across angle modes, and separate modules handle NORM/FIX/SCI formatting and S⇔D fraction, surd and π-multiple detection. An input state machine manages the cursor, SHIFT/ALPHA, memory and SETUP. The keypad is defined as data so it can be checked against the device, and React components render the display and keys. Automated tests cover the engine, interactive flows and rendering.
projects.outcome: A working COMP-mode replica that covers trig, logs, powers and roots, combinatorics, Pol/Rec, integration, differentiation, CALC, memory and error states, all backed by a test suite. The README sets out its limits: STAT, TABLE, CMPLX, BASE-N, EQN, MATRIX and VECTOR modes and ENG notation are not emulated.

projects.approach: Each sound is a procedural generator built on a shared DSP toolkit, feeding a per-orb channel strip (blend, AudioWorklet effects, EQ, Doppler, occlusion, air absorption, HRTF panner) into crossfading room convolvers, a compressor and a limiter. A sync layer diffs Zustand state into the imperative audio graph, while a single requestAnimationFrame loop drives motion, orbits, morphing and visual effects without React re-renders. The AI Composer is provider-agnostic: Claude, GPT and Gemini all answer in one Zod schema, and values are validated and clamped before they reach the mix.
projects.outcome: Aether is live as a web app on Cloudflare Workers, with 38 generators, 10 scenes, 8 rooms, an AI Composer for three providers, head tracking, recording and shareable mix links.

projects.problem: Ambient sound mixers usually play flat, looping recordings with a volume slider per track. Aether sets out to make a soundscape feel like a physical space: sounds placed around the listener in 3D, shaped by distance, rooms and walls, and generated so they never loop identically.

challenges: OpenAI blocks direct browser calls, so GPT requests go through the site's own Cloudflare Worker relay, which forwards the user's key without storing it and allows only the two endpoints the app needs.
Keeping many moving orbs, paths, particles and panner positions in sync at frame rate meant driving them from one animation loop outside React's render cycle.

projects.longDesc:
Aether is a visionOS-inspired audio workspace that runs in the browser. You sit at the centre of a 16-metre field and drag translucent sound orbs around you. Each orb is placed in 3D with HRTF binaural panning, so moving one changes where you hear it.

Every sound is synthesised live with the Web Audio API: 38 procedural generators covering rain, ocean waves, café murmur, fireplaces, singing bowls and more, built so they never repeat the same way twice. An optional Realism control blends licensed field recordings under ten of them. Distance cues, Doppler pitch shifts, wall occlusion and eight synthesised rooms, from cathedral to tiled bathroom, make the space feel physical.

You can also describe a place and have Claude, GPT or Gemini compose the mix with your own API key. The model picks the sounds, positions them, and chooses the room, musical key and colour palette. All three providers answer in a single shared schema that is validated before anything changes the mix.

On top of the audio there is a WebGL gradient background that reacts to the music, frosted-glass orbs, spectrum and spectrogram visualisers, snapshots you can morph between, drawn motion paths, webcam or phone head tracking, and share links that encode the whole mix.

projects.longDesc:
UsageNotch for Android puts your Claude, Codex, Gemini and Cursor usage limits on your phone. It is a companion to UsageNotch for Windows: the PC reads your providers, and the phone shows the same rings, limits, reset countdowns, budgets, alerts and history.

Pairing takes one QR scan with a built-in scanner that works without Google Play services, or you can paste a code or import a pairing file. Phone and PC share readings over the same Wi-Fi or a private VPN such as Tailscale. Optional internet sync encrypts each reading on the PC with AES-256-GCM and stores it in a secret gist in your own GitHub account. Your AI sign-ins stay on Windows.

The app is built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose in a liquid glass style, with a Classic alternative. It includes widgets that adapt to any size, a live countdown notification (a Live Update on Android 16), a Quick Settings tile, history kept on the phone, and a single usage score across providers. Readings stay visible when the PC is off, with estimates clearly labelled.

The APK is sideloaded and updates itself from GitHub Releases, checking each download against the published SHA-256 checksum and the installed app's signature.

projects.longDesc:
File Sharing, branded DropLink, is a browser tool for sending files directly between devices. Transfers run peer to peer over WebRTC data channels using PeerJS, so files travel from sender to receiver without being uploaded to a storage server, and no account is needed.

A sender opens a room and shares a six-character code or a QR code; the receiver enters or scans it, and incoming files must be accepted before they arrive. Devices on the same public network can also find each other on a discovery radar, which is switched off on cellular connections unless a private network name is set. Plain text can be sent as well.

Files are streamed in small chunks with backpressure on the data channel buffer, and where the browser supports it the receiver can choose a save folder so large files are written straight to disk. Small Vercel functions supply STUN servers, short-lived TURN credentials and a salted, hashed network scope, so raw IP addresses never leave the server.
